note: Station ids are <hole>AP<n> (SpatialAdjustApp.dc.html:169-186; the guides name 3AP1, 3AP2, 4AP1, 6AP1, 6AP2, 11AP2 and others). Read as the hole, then the area letters, then the station number: 3AP1 is 'hole 3, A P 1'.
The area name on its own, as in the caption 'Station-level rows for hole 3 of area AP'. Letters, not the word 'ap'. Runs after the station rule, so only a bare AP is left to match.
The product Spatial Adjust lives inside ('Spatial Adjust is a feature of IntelliDash'). The hyphen makes the model stress both halves instead of running them into one word.
The scan service that supplies the measured moisture ('TurfRad scan data', 'a TurfRad moisture scan'). Two words when spoken.

Toro Lynx, the central control that receives the pushed adjustments ('push the right percent adjustment to Lynx'). Said like 'links'; spelled that way so the model never spells it out or reads it as 'lunks'.
The feature name, as the guides write it (two words, both capitalised). Read correctly as written; listed so its spoken form is pinned and covered by the lexicon check line.
The column label 'Avg. VWC' and the toolbar summary 'Avg / High / Low'. Said as the full word; the abbreviation's full stop is consumed so it does not become a pause.
The editable column label '% Adj.' ('your own % Adj. value', 'Editing % Adj. queues the station'). Runs before the general percent rule, which needs a number in front of the sign.
Volumetric water content, as in 'Avg. VWC' and 'Target VWC'. Spelled out letter by letter, the way the column labels are read.
Evapotranspiration, as in 'today's ET' and 'Calculation ET'. Letters, so the model does not say 'et'. Case-sensitive and whole-word, so 'Et', 'ETo' and words containing ET are left alone.
A number followed by the percent sign: '17%' becomes '17 percent', '27.6%' becomes '27.6 percent'. The guides write 'percent' in captions and '%' in values such as 'Lynx receives 0%'.

Millimetres for Max Amount and Lynx Reference Amount values ('A 10 mm cap against a 3 mm reference'). The model can read 'mm' as 'em em' or as a hum; the unit is spelled out. Always plural: no guide writes 1 mm, so a script that needs it should say 'one millimetre'.
